title: Adab of knowledge
hook: a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet and teaches by asking

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of sleep, and your line: sleep with remembrance. Today, the manners of learning, which is what this whole path has been doing.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab tells it, in Sahih Muslim. They were sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a man walked in. Very white clothes. Very black hair. No dust of travel on him, and nobody there knew who he was. He sat right in front of the Prophet, rested his knees against the Prophet's knees, laid his palms on his thighs, and began to ask questions. Only later did the Prophet tell them who it was. Jibril, the angel, come to teach them their religion. He taught by asking.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `HE TAUGHT BY ASKING.`

segments.voice: That scene holds the adab of knowledge in its posture. Jibril came to teach, and he came looking like a student. He sat close. He was still. He asked, and listened. Respect for the one you learn from isn't flattery; it's how you sit. The Qur'an shows the same with a prophet. In al-Kahf, Moses meets a servant of Allah who has knowledge he doesn't, a man tradition calls al-Khidr. And Moses, himself a prophet, asks, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you can teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? He's told he'll need patience. He agrees, and then struggles to keep quiet. In Ta Ha, the Prophet himself is told to ask for more, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Nobody in these passages has finished learning. Then the sharp piece. Al-Saff, Pickthall again: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?" And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says, in paraphrase, that on the Day of Rising a person's feet won't move until they're asked about their life, their wealth, their body, and their knowledge: what did you do with it? Not how much did you know. Knowledge, in this adab, isn't a collection. It's a debt paid in action.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CAME AS A STUDENT.` · `A PROPHET ASKS TO FOLLOW.` · `MY LORD, INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `WHAT DID YOU DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: Look back over these last days, the kindlier word, the near side of the dish, leaving room, honoring the guest, the line before a trip, the last word before sleep, or anything else you've learned lately. Pick one you've heard and haven't yet done, and see exactly when it could happen. If you pray, you can say the line from Ta Ha: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
Adab of knowledge. The manners of learning: honor the one who teaches, stay humble enough to ask for more, and act on what you know. Today's word.
Your line: learn, then do. Knowing is the start, not the finish. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight, complete.

howItsDone: Muslim students are taught to honor their teachers, to recite "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge," and to treat knowledge as something to act on, citing the hadith of Jibril and the hadith of what a person did with what they knew.

chat.says: I've read so much about faith. Isn't knowing it the main thing?
options: It's a start. You'll be asked what you did with your knowledge, a hadith says.
Yes. The more you know, the better; doing can wait until you know it all.
Yes. Once you've learned enough, there's no need to keep asking for more.
chat.meaning: A hadith in al-Tirmidhi says each person is asked about their knowledge: what did you do with it? Knowledge is a debt paid in action.

Jibril.meaning: the angel Gabriel, who brought revelation

al-Khidr.meaning: the name tradition gives Moses' teacher in al-Kahf

al-Kahf.meaning: a surah of the Qur'an, The Cave

Ta Ha.meaning: a surah of the Qur'an, named for two Arabic letters

'Umar ibn al-Khattab.meaning: a close companion of the Prophet, later the second caliph
